1408.title: Shridhar's feast and the all-night jagran
1408.hook: a little girl tells a poor man to feed the whole village, and a Punjabi lane stays up all night for her
1408.carry: the mother feeds everyone who comes
1408.tomorrow: why throw sesame into a winter fire?
1408.howItsDone: Punjabi Hindu families hold a jagran, or jagrata, for Mata, often in thanks for a blessing: singers lead devotional songs through the night before a lit jyot, the neighbors are invited, and prasad is shared at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the mind is pure, the ganga is here: Ravidas at his bench, and the Ganga in a cobbler's bowl.
screen: `THE GANGA IN THE BOWL.`

segments.voice: In the hills of Jammu, the story goes, lived a poor man named Shridhar who loved the Goddess. One day a little girl came to him and said: hold a feast, a bhandara, and invite the whole village. Shridhar looked at his kitchen. He could barely feed himself. But he went door to door anyway, and the whole village came, far more people than his little house could hold. Today, what the girl did next, and why a Punjabi family still stays up all night for her.
screen: `A POOR MAN, A LITTLE GIRL.` → `FEED THE WHOLE VILLAGE.` → `HE COULD BARELY FEED HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: As the shrine's legend tells it, the girl served everyone herself, and every guest ate. One guest, a proud yogi named Bhairon, demanded meat and wine, and when she refused, he tried to grab her. She slipped away up the Trikuta mountain. Shridhar was heartbroken, until, the story says, she came to him in a dream and showed him her cave. That cave is Vaishno Devi, one of India's most visited shrines, where pilgrims climb day and night calling Jai Mata Di: victory to the Mother. Here's the teaching inside the story. In devotion to the Goddess, she is Mata, Mother: the one who feeds, and who comes in the smallest form, a little girl, to a man with nothing. That's why at Navratri many families wash the feet of young girls and feed them as the Goddess. And it's why a Punjabi family whose prayer was answered, a baby born, an illness passed, holds a jagran: a waking, a vigil. A picture of the Mother goes up in a tent in the lane. The lamp before her, the jyot, burns till dawn. Singers lead bhents, songs offered to her, and kids fall asleep on laps. At dawn comes prasad, food offered to her and then shared. And the whole lane is invited, like Shridhar's village. You don't thank the Mother and keep the blessing to yourself. What she gives, you set before her, then share with everyone who comes.

1409.title: Lohri, and the fire that carries gifts
1409.hook: a winter bonfire, a fistful of sesame and popcorn, and a song about an outlaw
1409.carry: agni carries what we give to god
1409.tomorrow: who gets the first of the harvest?
1409.howItsDone: On Lohri night, Punjabi families and neighbors light a bonfire, walk around it tossing in sesame, peanuts, rewri and popcorn, and celebrate a new baby's or new bride's first Lohri with special warmth.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother feeds everyone who comes: Shridhar's feast, and a jagran with the whole lane invited.
screen: `A NIGHT AWAKE FOR THE MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Cold enough to see your breath. A courtyard in Punjab, and in the middle, a bonfire taller than the kids around it. Someone presses a handful into your palm: sesame seeds, peanuts, a little hard sweet called rewri, a few pieces of popcorn. Everyone walks around the fire and throws a pinch in. The flames jump. Earlier, children went door to door singing, and came home with sweets and coins. The song is about an outlaw. Today, Lohri. Back on day one hundred fifty-two it got one line; today it gets the whole fire.
screen: `A BONFIRE IN THE COLD.` → `SESAME AND POPCORN IN THE PALM.` → `A SONG ABOUT AN OUTLAW.`

segments.voice: Lohri comes in the deep of winter, on the night before Maghi, the day tradition counts as the start of the sun's northward journey. First, the fire, and one of Hinduism's oldest teachings. The very first word of the Rig Veda, the oldest Hindu scripture, is Agni: fire. Its first hymn praises Agni as the priest who carries offerings to the gods. Whatever is poured into the fire, Agni takes up. At Lohri there's no priest and no chanting required, just a family tossing sesame and grain into the flames, some bowing as they go around. But the teaching is the same one: give to the fire, and the fire carries it to God. It's the same Agni who witnesses a Hindu wedding, as the couple walks around him. Then, the people. Lohri belongs to the Punjabi year itself, so Hindus, Sikhs and their neighbors keep it, each in their own way. It's loudest for a family with a first: a new baby's first Lohri, a new bride's first Lohri in her husband's home. The family's newest gift is brought to the fire with thanks. Then, the song. Children go door to door singing about Dulla Bhatti, a Punjabi Muslim folk hero remembered as an outlaw who, the story says, rescued a poor girl and saw her married as if she were his own daughter. So around a Hindu household's fire, kids sing about a Muslim outlaw with a good heart. Each family brings its own prayers, and the same heat reaches every face.

segments.voice: Cup one hand in your lap as if it holds sesame and popcorn, and think of one thing from this season you'd gladly give to the fire: a worry, a grudge, a tiredness carried too long. Hold it for a few breaths, then open the hand on an out-breath; if you pray, offer it to God, or to Agni, as the fire does.

1410.title: Vaisakhi and the first share
1410.hook: the wheat turns gold, and before anyone eats the new grain, the first of it goes back

1410.howItsDone: Hindus in Punjab keep Vaisakhi as the harvest and the solar new year, some bathing in a sacred river or temple tank at dawn, offering the first of the grain at the temple and giving to others; at home, food is offered before the shrine before anyone eats.

segments.voice: Months after the Lohri fire, the fields have changed color. The wheat planted in the cold stands gold and heavy, and the sickles are coming out. In the villages there's a fair: drums, swings, sugarcane, young men dancing bhangra with their arms up as if lifting the whole harvest. The day is Vaisakhi. And in Hindu homes there's a rule older than any fair: before anyone eats, the first share goes back. Today, where that rule comes from: a story Krishna tells about the very beginning.
screen: `THE WHEAT TURNS GOLD.` → `DRUMS, SWINGS, BHANGRA.` → `THE FIRST SHARE GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi takes its name from the spring month of Vaishakh. For Hindus in Punjab it's the harvest, and a new year by the sun. Some families bathe at dawn in a river or a temple tank, then take the first of the grain to the temple. Why the first? Picture the Bhagavad Gita's battlefield: two armies waiting, and Arjuna asking why he should act at all. Krishna answers by telling how things began. In paraphrase: when the Creator made human beings, he made them together with yajna, sacrifice, the giving back, and said: grow by this. Care for the gods, and they will care for you. From yajna comes rain, from rain comes grain. Then Krishna says something blunt. Whoever enjoys the gifts without giving anything back is a thief. The good eat what remains after the offering; those who cook only for themselves, he says, eat their own wrong. That's the teaching under a Hindu harvest. Food isn't simply earned. It's given, by the earth, the rain and God, and the first share goes back. It's why so many Hindu families set a plate before the shrine before anyone eats, and why what comes back is called prasad, a gift. On Vaisakhi it's why the first grain goes to the temple and to those who have less. The same street keeps another Vaisakhi too. For Sikhs, it remembers Guru Gobind Singh founding the Khalsa, told in their own words, and their langar feeds anyone who walks in. Two traditions, two reasons, and at harvest, an open hand on both sides of the street.
screen: `VAISAKHI: HARVEST AND A NEW YEAR` · `MADE TOGETHER WITH YAJNA` · `TAKE WITHOUT GIVING: A THIEF` · `THE FIRST SHARE GOES BACK` · then, large: `AN OPEN HAND, BOTH SIDES OF THE STREET.`

segments.voice: Picture tonight's plate in front of you. Before your hand reaches for it, pause. If you pray, offer it first, silently or with a word, to God or to Krishna, and let what comes back be prasad. If you don't pray, take one breath for where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that grew and cooked it. Rest in that pause now, so it's ready at dinner.

1411.title: Valmiki takes in Sita
1411.hook: a queen left alone at the forest's edge, and the poet who finds her
1411.carry: the ramayana was born from compassion
1411.tomorrow: why can't the mind let go?
1411.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Ram Tirath near Amritsar, honored in tradition as Valmiki's hermitage, and Valmiki's birthday is kept in Punjab with processions and devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakhi and the Gita's harvest rule: food is a gift; the first share goes back.
screen: `THE SAME DAY, EACH ITS OWN MEANING.`

segments.voice: A woman sits alone at the edge of a forest, crying. She is Sita, the queen of Ayodhya, and she's carrying a child. Ram has sent her away because of what people in the city were saying, and the brother who drove her here has gone back. Young students from a nearby hermitage hear her and run to tell their teacher. He comes out to her. He's Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana, and he finds the heroine of his own story weeping at his door. Today, Punjab's last stop: a place tradition calls that door.
screen: `SITA ALONE AT THE FOREST'S EDGE.` → `THE STUDENTS RUN FOR THEIR TEACHER.` → `VALMIKI COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: In the last book of Valmiki's Ramayana, in paraphrase, Valmiki speaks gently to Sita. He tells her he knows she has done no wrong. He brings her into his hermitage and gives her into the care of the women there, to be looked after like a daughter. Her twin sons, Lava and Kusha, are born there, and Valmiki teaches them the Ramayana; in the story, they sing it, their own father's story, before Ram himself. Why would the poet take her side when a whole city had turned on her? Go back to the start of his poem. In its first book, Valmiki watches a hunter shoot one of a pair of cranes as they call to each other. The bird falls, and its mate cries over it. Grief pours out of Valmiki in a new kind of measured line, and he realizes he has made the first shloka, the verse: his shoka, grief, became shloka. Then Brahma tells him to use that verse to tell Ram's story. That's the teaching. The Ramayana is born from karuna, compassion, and tradition honors Valmiki as the adi kavi, the first poet, for exactly that. The poet who wept for a bird is the one who takes in a weeping queen. And the place: tradition puts his hermitage at Ram Tirath, near Amritsar, with a temple and a sacred tank. In Punjab, the Valmiki community honors him with special devotion as Bhagwan Valmiki, with processions on his birthday.
screen: `VALMIKI SHELTERS SITA` · `A CRANE FALLS; GRIEF BECOMES VERSE` · `KARUNA: THE RAMAYANA'S ROOT` · `RAM TIRATH, NEAR AMRITSAR` · then, large: `THE FIRST POET TAKES HER IN.`

segments.voice: Think of a time when life turned hard and someone took you in: a friend's couch, a teacher's office, a grandparent's kitchen, a kind word at the right moment. Let that person come to mind, feel what it was like to be sheltered, and for a few breaths simply wish them well; if you pray, hold them before God. If life feels that hard right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

segments.voice: A forest hermitage. A king sits on the ground; his ministers turned on him and his enemies took his city. Beside him sits a merchant whose own wife and sons threw him out for his money. The strange part: the king keeps worrying about his old elephants and his treasury. segments.voice: Near the top of the year, each day now looks back at one part of the climb. Start with the Devi Mahatmya. The king is Suratha, the merchant Samadhi, the sage Medhas, and his answer is the whole book. The pull they feel, he says, is the goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that draws the minds of even the wise into confusion. Then he tells them who she is, through her stories: the goddess leaving the sleeping Vishnu so that he wakes to face two demons; the goddess given every god's weapon to face the buffalo demon Mahisha; the goddess who meets Shumbha and Nishumbha, with Kali springing from her brow. The same power that binds the mind, Medhas says, sets it free. The book ends not on a battlefield but by a river. They worship the goddess there, and she appears and asks what each wants. The king asks for his kingdom back, and she grants it. The merchant asks for the knowledge that loosens the grip of me and mine. She grants that too. Same question, two different answers. That's the Shakta teaching in one line: the pull of me and mine, maya, isn't outside the goddess. It is her power, so the way out runs through her too. And the question is an ordinary one: why does my mind keep going back to what hurt me? The book doesn't scold it. It sends you to the Mother, who holds the knot and its loosening.

1413.title: Ramakrishna's snake: Brahman and Shakti
1413.hook: is a snake lying still a different snake from the one that moves?

1413.howItsDone: Shakta devotees worship the goddess as the power that moves the world, reciting hymns such as the Saundarya Lahari and the Lalita Sahasranama, and calling her simply Mother.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FOUR-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Is a snake lying coiled in the sun a different snake from the one that slides off into the grass? Nobody would say so. Same snake, resting, then moving. That small picture is credited to Sri Ramakrishna, the temple priest of Dakshineswar, and the year used it to open a whole stretch of teaching. In the weeks after the Devi Mahatmya, the path stopped telling the goddess's stories for a while and asked what she is. Today's summit sit climbs back to that question: Shakti, as a way of thinking.
screen: `A SNAKE, COILED.` → `THE SAME SNAKE, MOVING.` → `WHAT IS THE GODDESS?`

segments.voice: Shakti means power: the power to act, to make, to move. In the teaching remembered from Ramakrishna, when the divine is thought of as still, beyond all doing, he called it Brahman. When it is thought of as creating, keeping and dissolving the world, he called it Shakti, the Mother. Not two things: one snake, at rest and in motion. Now take that picture to a hymn the year read. The Saundarya Lahari, a long poem to the goddess traditionally credited to Shankara, opens with a startling sentence. In paraphrase: Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create; without her, the god cannot so much as stir. A hymn of praise that starts by saying the great god can't move a finger on his own. That's the Shakta turn: power isn't a tool that someone holds. Power is the goddess herself. From up here, look how often the year came back to it. The goddess rising out of the gods' own blazing power in the Devi Mahatmya, every weapon handed over to her. The Rig Veda hymn where a goddess speaks for herself: I move with the gods, I bend the bow. The Lalita hymn that names the goddess as Shiva and Shakti in one form. Different texts, one thread: the world is not dead matter waiting for a spirit. It moves, and the moving is divine. Shakta and Shaiva teachers argue about how the two relate. But for a Shakta it changes an ordinary day: the busy, moving world, a kitchen, a commute, a body breathing, isn't a distraction from God. It's the Mother at work.
screen: `SHAKTI: POWER, THE POWER TO MOVE.` · `STILL, BRAHMAN. MOVING, THE MOTHER.` · `WITHOUT HER, SHIVA CANNOT STIR.` · `THE MOVING IS DIVINE.` · then, large: `ONE SNAKE.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle until it's mostly still, then notice what is still moving: the breath, the pulse in your hands, small shifts of balance. Don't stop any of it; let stillness and movement sit in one body, like the coiled snake and the moving snake, and if you pray, rest in the goddess as that movement.

segments.voice: A wandering beggar walks into a pine forest where proud sages live, and they don't recognize him. In the Tamil temple tradition of Chidambaram, the beggar is Shiva. The sages, furious, light a fire to destroy him and send a tiger out of it. He peels off its skin and wraps it round his waist. They send a snake. He hangs it round his neck like a garland. They send a snarling dwarf, and Shiva sets one foot on the dwarf's back, lifts the other, and dances. The sages fall silent, and bow. Today's summit sit goes back to that dance: Nataraja, the lord of the dance.
screen: `A TIGER: HE WEARS ITS SKIN.` → `A SNAKE: HE WEARS IT AS A GARLAND.` → `A DWARF: HE DANCES ON HIM.`

segments.voice: The bronze you've seen in a museum freezes that moment. Read it now all at once. In one hand, a small drum: the sound of things beginning. In the hand across from it, a flame: the ending, held level with the drum. Another hand is raised, palm out: do not fear. Under the planted foot lies the dwarf from the forest, named Apasmara, forgetfulness, held down but never killed. Tamil Shaiva teaching reads the whole figure as Shiva's five acts in the world: making, keeping, ending, concealing, and grace. And here's the heart of it. One arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and its hand points down to the lifted foot. That foot is grace, the refuge. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang, in paraphrase, that just to see that lifted foot would make a human birth worth having. So the teaching isn't only that beginnings and endings dance together, though they do: the drum doesn't wait for the flame. It's that inside all the turning, the god himself points to the way out. That's why a Bharatanatyam dancer salutes Nataraja before she begins: her dance is offered into his. And it's how a Shaiva meets a crowded week. A newborn and a goodbye, a new job and an ending: the drum and the flame aren't yours to balance. They're in his hands. Your part is to look where his hand points.
